content: This overview focuses on interventions for managing pain and subfertility in premenopausal women with clinically diagnosed endometriosis. It summarizes evidence from Cochrane systematic reviews on treatment options for these women. The primary outcomes related to pain included pain relief, clinical improvement or resolution, and recurrence of pain. Fertility-related outcomes included live birth, clinical pregnancy, ongoing pregnancy, miscarriage, and adverse events. The quality of the evidence was assessed using AMSTAR and GRADE methods, and findings were summarized in the text and additional tables. Pain Relief: 1. Gonadotrophin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) Analogues: A systematic review provided low-quality evidence suggesting that GnRH analogues were more effective than placebo or no treatment in relieving pain. 2. Ovulation Suppression: Moderate-quality evidence indicated that the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUD) was more effective than expectant management. Very low-quality evidence suggested that danazol was more effective than placebo. There was no consistent evidence of differences in effectiveness between oral contraceptives and goserelin, estrogen plus progestogen and placebo, or progestogens and placebo. However, the evidence in these comparisons was of low or very low quality. 3. Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs): Evidence regarding the effectiveness of NSAIDs for symptom relief compared to placebo was inconclusive. 4. Surgical Interventions: Moderate-quality evidence showed that laparoscopic surgery provided better pain relief compared to diagnostic laparoscopy alone. Very low-quality evidence suggested that excisional surgery reduced recurrence rates of endometriomata compared to ablative surgery. 5. Post-Surgical Medical Interventions: Two reviews found no evidence that post-surgical medical treatments improved pain outcomes. The evidence was of low or very low quality. 6. Alternative Medicine: One review found low or very low-quality evidence that auricular acupuncture was more effective than Chinese herbal medicine. Another review found no difference in effectiveness between Chinese herbal medicine and danazol. 7. Anti-TNF-α Drugs: A review found no evidence of a difference in effectiveness between anti-TNF-α drugs and placebo. The evidence was of low quality. Fertility Outcomes: 1. Medical Interventions: One review found very low-quality evidence that three months of GnRH agonist treatment improved clinical pregnancy rates in women undergoing assisted reproduction. No evidence of differences in effectiveness was found in comparisons of GnRH agonists versus antagonists, ovulation suppression versus placebo or no treatment, or pre-surgical medical therapy versus surgery alone. The evidence in these cases was of low or very low quality. 2. Surgical Interventions: Moderate-quality evidence indicated that laparoscopic surgery improved live birth and clinical pregnancy rates compared to diagnostic laparoscopy alone. Low-quality evidence suggested no difference in effectiveness between surgery and expectant management for endometrioma. Low-quality evidence indicated that excisional surgery resulted in higher clinical pregnancy rates compared to drainage or ablation of endometriomata. 3. Post-Surgical Medical Interventions: Two reviews found no evidence that post-surgical medical treatments improved clinical pregnancy rates. The evidence was of low or very low quality. 4. Alternative Medicine: A review comparing Chinese herbal medicine with gestrinone found no evidence of a difference in clinical pregnancy rates. The evidence was of low quality. Adverse Events: 1. GnRH analogues and danazol were associated with higher rates of adverse effects compared to placebo. 2. Depot progestagens were linked to higher rates of adverse events compared to other treatments. 3. Chinese herbal medicine was associated with fewer side effects compared to gestrinone or danazol. 4. Three reviews reported miscarriage as an outcome, but no differences were found between surgical and diagnostic laparoscopy, GnRH agonists and antagonists, or aspiration of endometrioma and expectant management. The evidence in all cases was of low quality. Authors' Conclusions: 1. For pain management in women with endometriosis, suppression of menstrual cycles using GnRH analogues, LNG-IUD, and danazol were effective interventions. Laparoscopic treatment and excision of endometriomata also improved pain outcomes. Evidence on NSAIDs was inconclusive, and post-surgical medical treatments showed no benefit for pain relief. 2. For fertility outcomes, three months of GnRH agonist treatment improved pregnancy rates in women undergoing assisted reproduction. Excisional surgery improved spontaneous pregnancy rates within 9–12 months compared to ablative surgery. Laparoscopic surgery improved live birth and pregnancy rates compared to diagnostic laparoscopy alone. Medical treatments did not improve clinical pregnancy rates. 3. Evidence on adverse effects was limited, but GnRH analogues, danazol, and depot progestagens were associated with higher rates of adverse events compared to other interventions.
